method_note: FAST MODE. Legal facts from AGD and the Federal Register of Legislation only; reused facts keep original dates. Brand facts from live weddedwonderland.com only. No competitor or third-party AI product sources.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2): 'Where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised celebrant, not being a minister of religion, it is sufficient if each of the parties says to the other, in the presence of the authorised celebrant and the witnesses, the words: "I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)"; or words to that effect.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Quote exactly in the script as the legal vow line. Each partner says it to the other. Deciding authority: the authorised celebrant, under AGD.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(1): where the authorised celebrant is a minister of religion, the marriage 'may be solemnised according to any form and ceremony recognised as sufficient for the purpose by the religious body or organisation of which he or she is a minister.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: One line: a religious elopement follows the minister's rite, so the template is for civil celebrants.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 46(1) (the monitum): where the authorised celebrant is not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination, the celebrant 'shall say to the parties, in the presence of the witnesses, the words: "I am duly authorised by law to solemnise marriages according to law. Before you are joined in marriage in my presence and in the presence of these witnesses, I am to remind you of the solemn and binding nature of the relationship into which you are now about to enter. Marriage, according to law in Australia, is the union of 2 people to the exclusion of all others, voluntarily entered into for life."; or words to that effect.'
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961 (compilation C2026C00129, 28 March 2026)
facts.use_note: Said by the celebrant, not the couple, before the vows. Quote exactly in the script.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: 'A celebrant must be physically present to solemnise a marriage, together with the parties and 2 witnesses.' On the day, 3 marriage certificates are signed by the couple, the celebrant and 2 witnesses over 18; the celebrant lodges the paperwork with the state or territory registry of births, deaths and marriages within 14 days.
facts.use_note: Minimum people at a legal Australian elopement: the couple, an authorised celebrant and 2 witnesses, all physically present. No video-link ceremony. Whether the celebrant can double as a witness is not sourced (N-02); write 'two people besides your celebrant'.

facts.claim: To marry in Australia you must, among other things: be at least 18; understand what marriage means and freely agree to marry; use specific words during the ceremony; give a NOIM to an authorised marriage celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding; and be married by an authorised marriage celebrant. You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident.
facts.use_note: Short checklist for the 'is it legal' section. NOIM timing re-read live 2026-11-22, unchanged.

facts.claim: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2) wording ends 'or words to that effect', and s 46(1) likewise. Nothing in s 45 or s 46 bars couples from adding their own vows; the Act sets the minimum words that must be said.
facts.publisher: Federal Register of Legislation, Marriage Act 1961
facts.use_note: Second sentence is our reading of the statute. Phrase as: 'your own vows go alongside the legal words, and your celebrant confirms the final wording'.

facts.claim: Attorney-General's Department: 'Overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant and cannot be registered in Australia. An overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was a valid marriage in the overseas country and would have been a valid marriage here.'
facts.use_note: Core of the 'abroad' section: an Australian celebrant reading this script overseas makes it symbolic. The legal step is done at home or under local law.

facts.claim: Our How to Write Wedding Vows page recommends about 150 words, about a minute out loud, with 300 words the most it suggests.
facts.quote: Aim for about 150 words, a minute out loud, and agree the length with your partner. ... So 150 words takes about a minute with pauses, and 300 words is the most we would suggest.
facts.use_note: House length line. The brief's '250 to 300 words, about two minutes' does NOT match this page; see C-01. Body read at /how-to-write-wedding-vows; canonical og:url is /planning/how-to-write-wedding-vows (published 2026-09-29, modified 2026-11-25), same title and hero image. Treat /planning/ URL as the parent vows page.

facts.claim: FAQ on the same page: about a minute each (130 to 150 words); two minutes, around 300 words, is about as long as guests follow comfortably; read aloud with a timer.
facts.quote: About a minute each, which is roughly 130 to 150 words at a calm ceremony pace. Two minutes, around 300 words, is about as long as guests follow comfortably. Agree a rough length with your partner so the two vows feel matched, then read yours aloud with a timer, because nerves change your pace.
facts.use_note: Use for the read-aloud length check. Two minutes / 300 words is a ceiling, not the target. Body read at /how-to-write-wedding-vows; canonical og:url is /planning/how-to-write-wedding-vows (published 2026-09-29, modified 2026-11-25), same title and hero image. Treat /planning/ URL as the parent vows page.

facts.claim: The page's method: write a messy first draft from your own memories before reading examples; five questions; five-part vow structure; the stranger test.
facts.quote: Write a messy first draft from your own memories before you read any examples. ... When did you first know you loved them? What do they do that nobody else would notice? Which single memory sums up the two of you? How has life changed since you met? What could you promise and still be keeping in ten years? ... If a stranger could say a line about their own partner, cut it. "You make me happy" fails, and "you leave one light on in the hallway for me" passes. Soulmate, partner in crime and other half belong to everyone, so cut them too.
facts.use_note: Natural fit for the AI prompt framework (feed your own answers to the five questions) and for editing out generic AI phrasing (stranger test). Link, do not reproduce in full. Body read at /how-to-write-wedding-vows; canonical og:url is /planning/how-to-write-wedding-vows (published 2026-09-29, modified 2026-11-25), same title and hero image. Treat /planning/ URL as the parent vows page.

facts.quote: "When you Google 'example wedding vows' you're stepping into years of tradition, other people's love, other people's celebrations," he said. "They're all awesome examples of how to party, but they're not you."
facts.use_note: Attributed quote from our own page; may be quoted with attribution to Josh Withers as said to Wedded Wonderland. Do not extend it to say he comments on AI. Body read at /how-to-write-wedding-vows; canonical og:url is /planning/how-to-write-wedding-vows (published 2026-09-29, modified 2026-11-25), same title and hero image. Treat /planning/ URL as the parent vows page.

facts.claim: Same page: your own vows come after the Australian legal words and must not contradict them; read from a card or vow book, never your phone.
facts.quote: Your vows come after the legal words and must not contradict them. Read from a card or a vow book, never your phone, and give your celebrant a spare.

facts.claim: AGD Get married page, re-read live 2026-11-26: to marry in Australia you must 'use specific words during the ceremony'; the page itself does not list the words. AGD says it gives general guidance, not legal advice, and to ask AGD or an authorised marriage celebrant.
facts.quote: To get married in Australia, you must: ... understand what marriage means and freely agree to marry - use specific words during the ceremony ... We can provide general guidance on marriage in Australia, but we can't give you specific legal advice. For guidance about getting married you should ask us or contact an authorised marriage celebrant.
facts.use_note: Unchanged since 2026-11-22 read (L-05, L-06, L-12 confirmed). The exact words are in the Act (L-01, L-03 via legislation.gov.au); AGD's page only says 'specific words'. Confirming authority: the authorised celebrant / AGD Marriage Law and Celebrants Section.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines (v6.0, Nov 2026) para 4.23: the parties must say the s 45(2) words to each other in the presence of the celebrant and witnesses.
facts.quote: The parties must say the following words to each other in the presence of the celebrant and the witnesses: “I call upon the persons here present to witness that I, A.B. (or C.D.), take thee, C.D. (or A.B.), to be my lawful wedded wife (or husband, or spouse)” or words to that effect.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for Authorised Celebrants (version 6.0, November 2026)
facts.use_note: Matches L-01 (Act s 45(2)). Read via Firecrawl extract of the AGD PDF (direct download blocked by proxy). Latest edition, listed on ag.gov.au publications 17 November 2026. Confirming authority: the authorised celebrant / AGD.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines para 4.24 'Can the couple personalise the vows?': the s 45(2) words are the minimum words the couple must exchange.
facts.quote: The words in subsection 45(2) are the minimum words which must be exchanged by the couple to ensure that they fully understand the nature of the ceremony and that they are marrying each other.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for Authorised Celebrants (version 6.0, November 2026)
facts.use_note: Official support for 'personal vows go alongside the legal words' (upgrades L-11 reasoning). Extract may have returned only the first sentence of 4.24; do not quote further text. Phrase: 'the legal words are the minimum; your own vows sit alongside them, and your celebrant confirms the final wording'.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines para 4.12: the monitum (s 46(1)) may be said as 'words to that effect', but the celebrant must not dilute or alter its meaning.
facts.quote: Subsection 46(1) of the Marriage Act requires that Commonwealth-registered marriage celebrants and state and territory officers authorised to solemnise marriages say the words set out in subsection 46(1) or ‘words to that effect’. This means there is some capacity to change certain words, provided a celebrant does not dilute the words or substitute words that alter the meaning of the words in subsection 46(1).
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for Authorised Celebrants (version 6.0, November 2026)
facts.use_note: The monitum is the celebrant's job, not the couple's; an AI draft should never rewrite it. Pair with L-03 for the full words.

facts.claim: AGD Guidelines para 4.20: under s 45(2), where a civil celebrant or state/territory officer solemnises, the parties must say the legal vows.
facts.quote: Under subsection 45(2), where a marriage is solemnised by an authorised state or territory officer or a Commonwealth-registered marriage celebrant (not being a minister of religion), the parties to the marriage must say the legal vows.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Guidelines on the Marriage Act 1961 for Authorised Celebrants (version 6.0, November 2026)
facts.use_note: Religious ceremonies follow L-02.

facts.claim: OAIC guidance on generative AI is addressed to organisations, not individuals. As best practice it recommends organisations do not enter personal information, particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools; once input, information is very difficult to track or control and potentially impossible to remove.
facts.quote: This new guidance is targeted at organisations that are deploying AI systems that were built with, collect, store, use or disclose personal information ... As a matter of best practice, the OAIC recommends that organisations do not enter personal information, and particularly sensitive information, into publicly available generative AI tools, due to the significant and complex privacy risks involved. ... Once personal information has been input into AI systems, particularly generative AI products, it will be very difficult to track or control how it is used, and potentially impossible to remove the information from the system.
facts.publisher: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
facts.use_note: Published 21 Oct 2024, modified 17 Jan 2025. Applies to entities under the Privacy Act, NOT to a couple typing into a chatbot. No legal claim applies to individuals: privacy section is advice only. Writer may say 'Australia's privacy regulator advises businesses not to put personal information into public AI tools, and the same caution is sensible at home' without implying a legal duty. Quotes from page body via Firecrawl search snippet of the official page.

facts.claim: No OAIC page found that gives individuals rules or guidance on entering their own personal information into AI chatbots (site search for individuals/AI/chatbot returned only organisation guidance, APP guidelines and submissions).
facts.use_note: Record of absence. Do not cite OAIC as giving advice to couples.

facts.claim: Traditional Wedding Vows page: Catholic and Church of England vows are fixed; most other ministers let you add a line; a civil celebrant allows almost anything once the legal words are said. Advice: say the old words exactly, then add two or three sentences of your own.
facts.quote: Catholic and Church of England vows are fixed, most other ministers will let you add a line, and a civil celebrant allows almost anything once the legal words are said. Jewish, Hindu, Muslim and Sikh rites keep their core ritual whole. Say the old words exactly as written, then add two or three sentences of your own, or put them in a reading or a letter.
facts.use_note: Published 2026-09-30, modified 2026-11-25. Live, not redirected. Link for religious or set wording; supports 'AI can help with your own lines, never rewrite a fixed rite'. Also live target of the redirected bible-verses vows URL (per orchestrator).
